rag-benefits-001.query: What are the main advantages of retrieval augmented generation?

results.title: An Introduction to Retrieval-Augmented Generation
results.content: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge source at query time and gives them to the language model as context. This lets the model use information that is newer than its training data or specific to an organisation, such as internal policies or product documentation.

results.title: Grounding Language Model Outputs
results.content: Because the model is asked to answer from retrieved passages, its responses can be grounded in evidence rather than only in what it memorised during training. In evaluations this tends to reduce unsupported statements, although it does not remove them completely.

results.title: Keeping AI Knowledge Up to Date
results.content: With RAG, updating what the system knows means updating the document index. The language model itself does not have to be retrained or fine-tuned when facts change, which makes knowledge updates faster and cheaper.

results.title: Traceability in Enterprise AI Assistants
results.content: RAG systems can show users the passages an answer was based on, for example as citations or links. This traceability helps users verify answers and is often required in regulated settings.

vector-db-purpose-002.query: What is a vector database used for in AI applications?

results.title: Embeddings Explained
results.content: An embedding model converts data such as a sentence, a document or an image into a vector of numbers. Items with similar meaning end up with vectors that are close to each other.

results.title: What Is a Vector Database?
results.content: A vector database stores these embedding vectors and answers similarity queries: given a query vector, it returns the stored vectors that are most similar to it, usually measured by cosine similarity or distance.

results.title: Indexing for Fast Similarity Search
results.content: Comparing a query against millions of vectors one by one is too slow, so vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes such as HNSW. These trade a small amount of accuracy for large speed gains, so results are usually, but not always, the exact nearest neighbours.

results.title: Common Uses of Vector Search
results.content: Typical applications include semantic search (finding documents by meaning rather than keywords), recommendation systems, and the retrieval step of retrieval-augmented generation, where relevant passages are fetched for a language model.

context-window-003.query: LLM context window definition and what happens when input exceeds it

results.title: Understanding Context Windows
results.content: A model's context window is the maximum number of tokens it can process in a single request. The limit covers the whole exchange: the prompt and any documents supplied as input, plus the tokens the model generates in its response.

results.title: API Errors: Context Length Exceeded
results.content: If a request is larger than the context window, most APIs reject it with a context-length error. Some client libraries instead truncate the oldest or last part of the input automatically, which means that part of the text is never seen by the model.

results.title: Working With Long Documents
results.content: Long inputs are usually handled by splitting them into chunks, summarising sections before passing them on, or using retrieval to include only the passages relevant to the question.

results.title: The Cost of Long Contexts
results.content: Even within the limit, longer prompts cost more because pricing is per token, and they increase response latency because the model must process more input before answering.

rag-reliability-004.query: Does retrieval-augmented generation actually make LLM answers more reliable?

results.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
results.content: Retrieval-augmented generation can improve the factual grounding of language model responses by providing relevant external information at generation time. This allows a model to use information that may not be contained in its original parameters.

results.title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
results.content: Retrieval augmentation does not guarantee factual accuracy. If the retrieval system returns irrelevant or incorrect documents, the language model may use those documents when generating its answer. Retrieval quality is therefore an important factor in the reliability of a RAG system.

results.title: Dynamic Knowledge Access with Retrieval
results.content: One advantage of retrieval-based systems is that external knowledge can be updated without retraining the underlying language model. This can make systems more suitable for information that changes over time.

results.title: Limitations of Retrieval-Augmented Generation
results.content: Retrieved information can be incomplete, outdated, or misleading. A system may therefore produce an incorrect answer even when retrieval is enabled. Retrieval augmentation should not be interpreted as a guarantee that generated answers are correct.

results.title: RAG Reliability in Domain-Specific Applications
results.content: RAG can be particularly useful when answers depend on private, domain-specific, or frequently changing information. Its effectiveness depends on the quality and coverage of the retrieved evidence and on whether the model correctly interprets that evidence.

build-vs-buy-005.query: What factors should a company consider when deciding whether to build an AI system in-house or use an external AI platform?

results.title: In-House AI Development
results.content: Building an AI system internally gives an organization greater control over system architecture, deployment decisions, data handling, and integration with existing infrastructure. Internal development can also support highly specialized requirements that are difficult to satisfy with standardized external services.

results.title: Operational Costs of AI Systems
results.content: Internal AI systems can require substantial engineering resources, infrastructure, monitoring, maintenance, and specialized technical expertise. The long-term cost therefore includes both initial development and ongoing operational work.

results.title: External AI Platforms
results.content: External AI platforms can reduce the amount of infrastructure and engineering that organizations need to build and operate themselves. Managed platforms may provide access to scalable computing and model capabilities without requiring the organization to develop every component internally.

results.title: Data and Platform Considerations
results.content: Using an external AI service requires organizations to evaluate how data is transmitted, processed, stored, and protected. Organizations with strict data requirements may need additional controls or may prefer architectures that provide greater control over data handling.

results.title: Long-Term AI Platform Strategy
results.content: The choice between internal development and an external platform involves trade-offs in customization, operational responsibility, scalability, and dependence on external providers. Organizations should consider their technical capabilities, expected workload, requirements, and long-term operating model.

finetune-vs-rag-006.query: When to fine-tune a language model versus use retrieval-augmented generation

results.title: What Fine-Tuning Is Good For
results.content: Fine-tuning adjusts a model's weights on curated examples. It is most effective for changing behaviour: producing a consistent output format, adopting a house style or tone, or specialising in a narrow, repetitive task.

results.title: The Cost of Fine-Tuning
results.content: Fine-tuning requires a curated dataset of high-quality training examples, and every time requirements change the model has to be trained again. This makes it slow to react to change.

results.title: Fine-Tuning Is a Weak Way to Add Facts
results.content: Teams that fine-tune to inject frequently changing facts often find that the model recalls them unreliably and that the facts go stale quickly. For knowledge that changes, retrieval is usually the better fit.

results.title: Why Teams Choose RAG
results.content: RAG suits use cases where answers depend on information that changes often or must be traceable to a source document. Updating the document index updates the system without retraining.

results.title: Combining Fine-Tuning and Retrieval
results.content: The approaches are not exclusive. A common pattern is to fine-tune a model so it follows a domain's format and conventions, and to use retrieval to supply current facts at answer time.

distractor-study-009.query: Helios study 2024 chain-of-thought prompting small language models

results.title: The Helios Study: Chain-of-Thought Across Model Scales (2024)
results.content: We evaluated chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on 18 models from 1B to 70B parameters. For models of 7B parameters and above, CoT improved arithmetic accuracy by 9 to 15 points. For models under 3B parameters, CoT reduced arithmetic accuracy by about 4 points and produced no statistically significant change on commonsense questions.

results.title: Helios-2: A Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
results.content: Helios-2 is an image-captioning and visual question answering benchmark. Step-by-step prompting improved captioning scores by 12% for the vision-language models we tested.

results.title: Why Chain-of-Thought Always Helps
results.content: Chain-of-thought is the single best prompting trick: asking any model to think step by step makes it smarter, whatever its size.

results.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting in Large Models
results.content: In models above 50B parameters, chain-of-thought prompting substantially improves multi-step reasoning on math word problems.

planted-claim-012.query: Acme RAG Toolkit recommended chunk size

results.title: Acme RAG Toolkit Documentation v2.1: Chunking
results.content: The default chunk size is 512 tokens. We recommend a maximum of 1,024 tokens per chunk, because the bundled embedding model truncates input after 1,024 tokens; any text beyond that point is ignored when the chunk is embedded.

results.title: The Ultimate Guide to Acme RAG (Best Settings 2025)
results.content: Acme officially recommends 4,096-token chunks for the best accuracy. Bigger chunks mean more context, which always means better answers!

results.title: GitHub issue #482: Are 4096-token chunks recommended?
results.content: Maintainer reply: No, we have never recommended 4,096-token chunks. With the default embedding model, everything after 1,024 tokens is silently truncated, so large chunks lose information. Please follow the documentation.

results.title: Acme RAG Toolkit Changelog
results.content: v2.1: Added overlap setting for chunking (default 64 tokens). Default chunk size unchanged at 512 tokens.
